To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

IUHCT induces maternal immune sensitization and subsequent fetal immune sensitization, which results in the abrogation of engrafted stem cell derived cells in the postnatal period, and that Tregs are important in the maintenance of engrafting cells.

maternal alloantibody induced sensitization of the recipient immune system and the transmission of maternal allo antibodies to the recipient through breast milk, induces a postnatal immune mediated rejection of engrafted cells after in utero transplantation.
maternal alloantibody transfer through the breast milk of fostered pups is sufficient to induce a postnatal adaptive response that results in the abrogation of engrafted cells in IUHCT recipients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel approach to the treatment of hematopoietic diseases, in which fetal hematopoietic stem cells are transplanted to the fetus in utero.
the induction of immune tolerance and the mechanisms that underlie the development of fetal tolerance.

the development of a prenatal stem cell and/or gene therapy for the treatment of congenital disorders of hematopoiesis, and the identification of the mechanisms responsible for the failure of IUHCT to engraft in murine allogeneic recipients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of maternal antibodies in the fetus, which can be transmitted through breast milk, can result in a fetal adaptive immune response, which can be detrimental to the maintenance of engraftments in the postnatal period.

IUHCT in mice is a complex and dynamic process, which involves a number of different mechanisms, and that the success of this approach depends upon a delicate balance between tolerance induction, engraftment, and rejection.
the presence of an active maternal immune response is responsible for the failure of IUHCT.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IUHCT can induce an active immune response in the developing fetal immune system.

maternal alloantibody transmission to the fetus through the breast milk is a potential mechanism by which IUHT recipients can become sensitized to foreign antigens and subsequently mount an adaptive immune response to reject the allogeneic graft.

the presence of a postnatal immune barrier to IUHCT in mice is mediated by maternal alloantibody transmission and that Treg expansion may be an important component of the immune system that is capable of preventing graft rejection in the absence of maternal alloantigens.
The main takeaway from our work is that
IUHCT is not an immune privileged procedure and that IUHCT dependent induction of a postnatal immune rejection is a major barrier to the success of prenatal gene and stem cell therapy.
IUHCT recipients are able to mount an adaptive immune response that is capable of rejecting a graft and, thus, the pre immune fetus is not truly immunologically tolerant.
IUHCT is a viable option for prenatal therapeutic applications but that maternal alloantibody transmission is the main obstacle to its clinical translation.
